paragraphs: The laws are inflexible and cannot adapt themselves to circumstances. In certain cases this may make them disastrous, and at a time of crisis cause the ruin of the State. The order and slowness of the forms they prescribe require a stretch of time that circumstances sometimes refuse. A thousand cases may arise for which the legislator has made no provision, and part of being foresighted, and a very necessary part, is to know that everything cannot be foreseen.
It is wrong, therefore, to want political institutions so strong that it becomes impossible to suspend their operation. Even Sparta let its laws lapse.

Still, only the gravest dangers can outweigh the danger of altering the public order, and the sacred authority of the laws should be halted only when the existence of the country itself is at stake. In these rare and obvious cases, a special act provides for the public safety by placing it in the hands of the worthiest man. How this is done depends on the kind of danger.

Sometimes the remedy is simply a more active government. Then power is gathered in the hands of one or two of its members, and what changes is not the authority of the laws but only the way they are administered. But sometimes the peril is such that the machinery of the laws stands in the way of saving the State. Then the answer is to appoint a supreme ruler, who silences all the laws and for a moment suspends the sovereign authority. In such a case no one can doubt what the general will is, and it is clear that the people’s first intention is that the State should not perish. So suspending the legislative authority is in no sense abolishing it. The magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak. He dominates it, but he cannot represent it. He can do anything except make laws.

The Roman senate took the first course when it used a consecrated formula to charge the consuls with seeing to the safety of the Republic. The second course was taken when one of the two consuls appointed a dictator,[1] a custom Rome had borrowed from Alba.

In the early years of the Republic, Rome turned to the dictatorship very often. The State was not yet on a footing firm enough to stand by the strength of its constitution alone. The morals of the time made many precautions needless that would have been necessary in other periods. Nobody feared that a dictator would abuse his authority or try to hold it past his term. Quite the opposite: so much power seemed a burden to the man who wore it, and he hurried to lay it down, as if standing in for the laws were too troublesome and too dangerous a post to hold on to.

So what makes me criticize the careless use of this supreme magistracy in the earliest times is not the danger that it would be abused but the danger that it would be cheapened. It was used freely for elections, dedications and mere formalities. That risked making it less fearsome when it was truly needed, and teaching men to treat as empty a title they had only ever seen used at empty ceremonies.

Near the end of the Republic, the Romans had grown more wary, and they were as unreasonably stingy with the dictatorship as they had once been generous. It is easy to see that their fears had no foundation. The capital was too weak to be a threat, and that protected it from the magistrates in its midst. A dictator might in some cases defend public liberty, but he could never endanger it. And the chains of Rome would be forged not in Rome itself but in her armies. How feebly Marius resisted Sulla, and Pompey resisted Caesar, showed clearly what authority at home could expect to achieve against force from abroad.

This mistake led the Romans into serious blunders. One example is their failure to appoint a dictator during the Catilinarian conspiracy. Only the city itself was involved, plus at most a province of Italy, and the unlimited authority the laws gave a dictator would have let him dispose of the conspiracy quickly. As it was, the plot was crushed only through a run of lucky accidents that human prudence had no right to count on.

Instead the senate settled for handing all its power to the consuls. To act effectively, Cicero therefore had to go beyond his powers on a matter of life and death. In the first rush of joy his conduct was approved, but later he was rightly made to answer for the blood of citizens spilled against the laws. No one could ever have said that of a dictator. But the consul’s eloquence won the day. Roman though he was, he loved his own glory more than his country, and he looked less for the most lawful and secure way of saving the State than for a way to claim all the honor of saving it himself.[2] So he was rightly honored as the liberator of Rome, and rightly punished as a lawbreaker. However brilliant his recall may have been, it was undoubtedly an act of pardon.

However this weighty trust is conferred, its term should be set very short and made impossible to extend. The crises that call for it end quickly, either in the State’s ruin or in its rescue. Once the immediate need is past, the dictatorship turns into either tyranny or a dead letter. At Rome dictators held office for six months only, and most of them resigned before the time was up. With a longer term, they might well have tried to stretch it further, as the decemvirs did when they were elected for a year. A dictator had time only to meet the need for which he was chosen, and none to think up other projects.
